rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

Fireflies flash in patterns that are specific to each species. A male of one species, for example, emits a single long flash every few seconds, whereas another produces a rapid series of short pulses. Females respond only to the pattern of their own species, which prevents them from wasting time on males that cannot father their offspring.
rw1.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It disputes the claim that fireflies flash in patterns.
It provides examples of the species-specific patterns mentioned in the previous sentence.
It explains why female fireflies do not flash.
It describes how male fireflies compete for food.

rw1.why: The speech weighs on Isidore like a stone, but at the end he realises he does not need it, which shows a shift from anxiety to confidence. The passage does not criticise the guests, and he is not unprepared.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original short story. Isidore has been asked to give a speech at his retirement dinner.

Isidore had written the speech three times and burned two of them. The third lay folded in his jacket, and he could feel it there as he stood, like a stone in a shoe. Forty years of ledgers and no one in the room had ever asked him what he thought about anything but numbers. He cleared his throat, and a hush fell, and he realised, with a surprise that was almost joy, that he did not need the paper at all.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show a character's movement from anxiety to unexpected confidence
To explain the career that Isidore had before retiring
To criticise the people attending the dinner
To show that Isidore is unprepared for the occasion

rw1.why: The text reports that much of the benefit seemed to be relief of withdrawal. It does not say decaffeinated coffee is better, that drinkers always know their dose, or that caffeine has no effect on anyone.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about coffee.

Coffee drinkers often say that they feel more alert after a cup, and the caffeine in it is widely credited for this. But researchers who gave regular drinkers either caffeine or an identical-tasting decaffeinated drink found that much of the benefit disappeared in those who were not told what they had been given and who had gone without caffeine for a day. The effect of the first cup, the researchers concluded, is largely the relief of withdrawal rather than a true boost.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Much of the alertness regular drinkers feel from coffee may come from relief of withdrawal rather than a real boost.
Decaffeinated coffee is more effective than regular coffee.
Coffee drinkers are always aware of the amount of caffeine they take.
Caffeine has no effect on anyone who drinks it.

rw1.why: The text says English borrowed words with foods but that words also travel in the other direction. It makes no claim of most borrowings, about how often foods are named, or that borrowed words are never changed.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original essay about the history of a language.

English has borrowed words from dozens of languages, and many of them arrived with the foods they named: pasta from Italian, kebab from Turkish, ketchup from a Chinese dialect. Yet borrowing is rarely a one-way street. Words that travelled in the opposite direction, such as the English football and computer, are now heard in languages around the world, often adapted to local sounds.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: English has borrowed more words than any other language.
Foods are named more often than other things in English.
English both borrows words from other languages and lends words to them.
English words are never changed when they are borrowed.

Text 1

Some urban planners argue that cities should limit building heights to preserve neighbourhood character. They say that low-rise streets encourage walking and give residents a sense of belonging.

Text 2

An economist who studies housing argues that height limits restrict the supply of homes in cities where demand is high, driving up prices. She suggests that cities could protect character through design rules while still permitting taller buildings.
rw1.q: Based on the texts, how would the economist in Text 2 most likely respond to the planners' proposal in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that height limits are the best way to preserve character
By arguing that cities should ignore neighbourhood character entirely
By claiming that low-rise streets discourage walking
By saying that height limits have costs that the planners do not consider and that other measures could protect character

Lindqvist suggested that the colony's flexibility depends on a minority of individuals willing to deviate from the group.

a large stock of rare books.

The following text is adapted from an original essay about the history of navigation.

Before the invention of the marine chronometer, sailors could find their latitude by the stars but not their longitude, and ships were regularly wrecked on coasts they believed to be far away. The problem was so serious that in 1714 the British government offered a large prize to anyone who could solve it. The solution, a clock that kept accurate time at sea, came from a carpenter with no formal training.
rw2h.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It conveys the seriousness of a problem that the passage goes on to show was solved.
It explains how latitude was calculated before the chronometer.
It argues that the British government was responsible for the wrecks.
It describes the training of the carpenter who invented the clock.

rw2h.why: Selwyn lets the boy fail in private and nods toward the shore as if nothing had gone wrong, which shows tact and patience. He is not mocking the boy, and the passage does not suggest reluctance to learn or discuss his fishing.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is from an original novel. Selwyn, an old fisherman, is watching a young stranger attempt to row his boat.

The boy pulled too hard on the left oar, and the boat turned slowly in a circle, as boats will for the first hour of anyone's life. Selwyn let him. It was a kind of courtesy, he thought, to let a person fail in private, even if the privacy was only a matter of keeping one's face still. When the boy looked up, flushed and furious, Selwyn merely nodded toward the shore, as though they had both agreed on the destination all along.
rw2h.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To suggest that Selwyn is amused by the boy's failure
To show that the boy is reluctant to learn to row
To explain why Selwyn no longer fishes
To illustrate Selwyn's patient, tactful way of treating someone who is learning

Some linguists propose that all human languages share a deep grammatical structure, which explains why children everywhere learn their first language so quickly and with so little instruction.

A researcher who studies children's speech argues that children are exposed to far more language than the first view assumes, and that they are skilled at detecting statistical patterns in what they hear. rw2h.q: Based on the texts, how would the researcher in Text 2 most likely respond to the proposal in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that children receive little exposure to language
By denying that children learn language quickly
By claiming that languages share no features
By offering a different explanation for the speed with which children learn language

rw2h.why: The text reports ongoing neuron formation and a possible role in keeping memories distinct. The rate declines, the role is still debated, and blocking the neurons did affect memory.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

The long-standing view that the brain stops generating neurons in adulthood has been revised. Studies of a region involved in memory show that new neurons continue to form throughout life, though at a declining rate. Their role is still debated, but experiments in which the formation of new neurons was blocked found that animals had difficulty telling apart similar situations, suggesting that the new cells help the brain keep distinct memories from blurring together.
rw2h.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The brain produces neurons at an increasing rate with age.
Memory is unaffected by the number of neurons in the brain.
Adult brains continue to produce neurons, which may help distinguish similar memories.
Researchers have agreed on the exact role of new neurons.

rw2h.why: The text says X-rays show that the artist first painted a tense figure and then revised it to create calm. It does not say the work is a forgery, that he kept the first idea, or that its colours are admired.

The following text is from an original essay about a famous painting.

The painting has long been admired for the serenity of its central figure. Yet X-rays have revealed that the artist first painted her with a clenched fist and a turned head, as though about to leave the room. He then painted over this version, opened the hand and lowered the gaze. The calm for which the work is celebrated was not the artist's first idea; it was an achievement of revision.
rw2h.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The serenity admired in the painting resulted from the artist's revision of an earlier, more tense design.
X-rays show that the painting is a forgery.
The artist intended the figure to look as if she were leaving.
The painting has been admired chiefly for its colours.
